name: Ancient South Arabian, Hadramitic dialect
confidence_why: Hadramitic survives only in consonantal inscriptions with no reading tradition, and Nebes and Stein (2004) state that no conclusions are possible about the accent of Ancient South Arabian, which Kogan and Korotayev (1997) match by giving no stress statement for Sayhadic at all, so the stress of this language is unknown rather than disputed.
catalog_citation: Nebes, Norbert & Peter Stein. 2004. Ancient South Arabian. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, ch. 15, 454-487. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
catalog_locator: ch. 15, sec. 3.3 'Vowels', pp. 458-459 (archive.org, pp. 482-483; text copy)
catalog_quote: Apart from these few hints, practically nothing is known about the vocalization of the Ancient South Arabian texts preserved for us. The question of a possible differentiation of syllables according to vowel quantity, therefore, likewise cannot be answered with certainty, nor are any broad conclusions possible concerning the accentual relationships of Ancient South Arabian.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (42.9 MB, text) and its extracted text copy. The quoted passage is present verbatim: the text (sec. 3.3 'Vowels', book pp. 458-459), and independently re-extracted from the PDF text at pp. 482-483 ('..nor are any broad conclusions possible concerning the accentual relationships of Ancient South Arabian.'). Only a running page header ('ancient south arabian 459') intervenes at the page break; wording, order and punctuation match the report exactly. Surrounding section read: 3.2.3 Glides (w/y as matres lectionis -> /o:/, /e:/), 3.3 Vowels (plene -w/-y probably long /u:/ /i:/; otherwise vocalization unknown; vowel quantity and accent indeterminable), 3.4 Sabaic variation (s/z alter…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule can be stated: Hadramitic (like all Ancient South Arabian) is known only from a purely consonantal script with no reading tradition, so vowels, vowel quantity and the position or nature of the accent are unrecoverable; the authors explicitly decline any conclusion about accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (accent as a whole declared indeterminable).
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only accent-related remark anywhere in the accessible literature is Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224 (Hetzron vol.), a speculation that the Minaic non-etymological h 'was caused by a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)', with conditions unknown; Nebes & Stein 2004: 459-460 instead read such h-spellings (incl. the Hadramitic determinate ending -hn) as possible plene writings of a long vowel. Neither yields a stress position.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is made for Ancient South Arabian as a whole (Sabaic-based description covering Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic, Hadramitic); epigraphic corpus only, no spoken or recited forms exist.
new_statements.identity_note: hadr1235 is the extinct epigraphic language of the kingdom of Hadramawt (c. 8th c. BC - 4th c. AD), written in the purely consonantal South Arabian musnad script with no reading tradition; it is NOT modern Hadrami Arabic (hadr1236, ISO ayh). The quoted statement is made by Nebes & Stein for 'Ancient South Arabian' as a whole (Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic, Hadramitic = Glottolog family sayh1236), with Sabaic as the descriptive base; it applies to Hadramitic a fortiori (smaller corpus, same script). The one Glottolog 'descriptive' reference attached to hadr1235 in our source list (Walker 1978, Lahu funerary chants, JRAS) is a Glottolog mis-attachment and has nothing to do with this language. The earlier scan's pointer (Stein 2011 in Weninger) is the right modern authority but could not be opened; its 2004 predecessor by the same author (with Nebes) was opened instead.

sources.note: Phonology pp. 222-224 covers consonants (conventional table, 'dead languages without oral tradition') and vowels ('we cannot draw any direct information about Sayhadic vowels'); no stress/accent section. Sole mention of stress (p. 224): Minaic non-etymological h 'is thought.. caused by a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)', conditions unknown -- Minaic only, no location rule, nothing on Hadramitic.
